speaker: Terence Tao
title: Terence Tao: Hardest Problems in Mathematics, Physics & the Future of AI (#472)
question: In theoretical mathematics, how does constructing a counterexample to an artificially modified version of a hard equation actually help you solve the original problem?
guest: It provides what's called an obstruction in mathematics. What I did was turn off certain parts of the equation—usually when you turn off certain interactions, it makes an equation less nonlinear, more regular, and less likely to blow up. But I found that by turning off a very well-designed set of interactions, I could force all the energy to blow up in finite time. What that means is that if you want to prove global regularity for the actual Navier-Stokes equation, you must use some feature of the true equation that my artificial equation does not satisfy. So it rules out certain approaches. The thing about math is it's not just about taking a technique that is going to work and applying it; you also need to avoid taking the techniques that don't work. For really hard problems, there are often dozens of ways you might think could apply, and only after a lot of experience do you realize there's no way those methods will work. Having these counterexamples for nearby problems saves you a lot of time because you're not wasting energy on things you now know cannot possibly ever work.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A counterexample to a modified equation mostly helps by ruling out proof strategies: it shows which methods cannot possibly solve the original problem, and so narrows where a real proof must come from.

The logic is this. A proof technique typically uses only certain features of an equation, such as an energy conservation law, scaling symmetry, or standard function-space estimates. If you build a modified equation that keeps all those features but for which the desired result fails, then no argument relying only on those features can prove the original statement, since the same argument would "prove" something false about the modified equation.

The best-known example is Terence Tao's 2014 work on the Navier–Stokes equations. He constructed an "averaged" version that obeys the same energy identity and harmonic-analysis estimates, yet has solutions that blow up in finite time. So any proof of global regularity for the true equations must exploit finer structure specific to the real nonlinearity.

Such constructions can also help positively: the blow-up mechanism itself suggests a blueprint for attacking the original equation, should a counterexample exist there too.

models.answer: Constructing a counterexample to a modified equation acts as a diagnostic filter that rules out entire classes of doomed proof strategies while isolating what truly matters in the original problem. When mathematicians alter a hard equation—as Terence Tao famously did with an averaged three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equation—they deliberately preserve its coarse structural features, such as conservation laws, scaling symmetries, and standard function-space bounds. Because any proof relying solely on those shared properties would apply equally to the modified version, a counterexample erects a formal barrier: it proves that standard, broad-brush tools cannot settle the conjecture, steering researchers away from dead ends and pinpointing the finer algebraic or geometric structures that any valid proof must exploit. Conversely, if the original conjecture is actually false, the artificial counterexample supplies a concrete failure mechanism—such as a self-sustaining energy cascade across scales—that mathematicians can attempt to adapt to the stricter constraints of the true equation.

Most standard analytic tools, such as energy estimates or scaling bounds, are blind to fine algebraic details; they apply equally to the true equation and to a carefully altered cousin sharing the same coarse symmetries and conservation laws. The best-known example is Terence Tao's 2014 paper on an "averaged" Navier–Stokes equation. models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A counterexample to a modified equation can show exactly where a proposed proof needs a property of the original equation. If the same argument would also prove a claim that fails for the modified equation, the step that breaks can point you toward a hypothesis or structural feature you need to use.

For example, suppose you want to prove that the solution of \(y'=y\) with \(y(0)=1\) stays positive. If you drop the initial condition, \(y=0\) is a counterexample. That tells you the differential equation alone cannot guarantee positivity. It also suggests a route to the proof. Since \((e^{-t}y)'=0\), the initial condition fixes \(e^{-t}y=1\), so \(y=e^t>0\).

The counterexample helps by narrowing the search for a proof. It directly refutes the original claim only if that claim logically implies the claim the counterexample disproves.

The construction can also suggest a way forward. If you can identify how the modified equation allows blowup, you can ask whether a feature of the original, such as a cancellation between terms, blocks that mechanism. That gives you a concrete claim to investigate. Ruling out that one mechanism would be progress, though a full proof would still have to rule out every possible route to blowup.
